It is in enterprise research preview, with no published benchmarks, size or pricing yet. The post Bland Launches Tofu-1, a Full-Duplex Speech-to-Speech Model for Calls appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, has released Tofu-1 , a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview. The Tofu-1 speech-to-speech model targets calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines. It listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out, with no transcript between. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . What is Tofu-1? Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models. How does Tofu-1 differ from a cascade voice agent? Most voice agents are cascades. They turn speech into text, pass it to a language model, then turn the reply back into speech. Tofu-1 listens to the audio directly , so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland has not published the internal architecture. Audio understanding Bland lists 3 audio skills on its product page: Speaker tracking: tells speakers apart and works out who each one is addressing. Noise separation: separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones. Paralinguistics: hears hesitation, frustration and urgency. Full duplex and thinking while talking Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early. Scene generation Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise. What is Bland’s ‘TV Test’? The TV Test asks one question: can the model follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene? TV audio is often louder than the caller. Bland marks its TV Test walkthrough as illustrative, not recorded model output. How does Tofu-1 compare with other full-duplex models? FDB results use different benchmark versions and are not directly comparable. How can teams access Tofu-1? Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises. Bland names banking, healthcare, insurance and government as target sectors. The sign-up form asks for monthly call volume, from under 1,000 to 50,000+. Key Takeaways Tofu-1 is Bland’s first full-duplex speech-to-speech model, built for noisy calls. It hears audio directly: speakers, background noise and caller emotion. The only number is self-reported: over 92% could not spot it in screenings. No size, latency, pricing or benchmarks yet; rivals publish latency and tool-use scores. Access is a closed enterprise preview, with Bland citing January availability. Check out the Tofu-1 product page , the launch post on X and the research preview sign-up . The post Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp , a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy . Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace , an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR What it is: A DSPy optimizer ( WeightSpace ) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp , needs DSPy 3.5. Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head. Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU). Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points. Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor. Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8. Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models. What is weight-space programming? Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out. It averages 2x faster than v1, completes 82% of 478 internal web tasks, and learned to batch actions through latency-penalized RL. The post Hark Releases Handoff², a 2x Faster Computer-Use Agent for Hark Pro appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Hark has released Handoff² , the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app. The Hark Handoff 2 computer-use agent finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original, on average. Hark states that the gains come from reinforcement learning (RL) that penalized wasted turns and latency. For teams building browser agents, it is a case study in training for speed, not only accuracy. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Runs on: Hark’s cloud. Each request gets a dedicated virtual computer. Users reach it from web, iOS and Android. No local or quantized option. Performance: 82% task completion on Hark’s 478-task internal benchmark, about 2x faster end to end than v1. Best: 93.8% on Hark’s internal alignment benchmark (v1: 90.3%). Worst: 82% browsing completion still trails Claude Opus 5.5 (max), by up to 5 points, in the same harness. Bottom line (best): Up to 3.8x faster flight booking and more than 5x faster long research. Bottom line (worst): Every Handoff² number is self-reported. No third-party score exists yet. What is Hark Handoff²? Handoff² is a computer-use agent from Hark that operates websites the way a person does. It clicks, types and scrolls on live pages instead of calling APIs. Hark previewed Handoff in August and shipped it in Hark Pro in October. Since then, Hark says it has logged over 5.6M browsing sessions and handled over $20M in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications. How does Handoff² get 2x faster? Hark co-evolved 2 things: the agent harness and the RL training recipe. The new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn. Training then penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency. The model learned 3 habits: Batch actions, such as filling several form fields in 1 turn. Group repeated action patterns into reusable composite actions. Reuse those composites as the task continues. Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, file system and terminal. The model outputs cursor and keyboard actions aimed at screen coordinates. Because savings stack per turn, gains grow on longer, browsing-heavy tasks. How fast is Handoff² compared with Handoff? Hark reports these speedups over v1 : Average: about 2x faster end to end. Flight booking: up to 3.8x faster. Long research tasks: more than 5x faster. Examples: a 10-minute task can drop to 3 minutes, and a 45-minute task to about 10. What do the Handoff² benchmarks show? Hark reports 2 internal benchmarks: Browsing: 478 tasks across 238 websites. Handoff² completes 82%, up from 73% for v1. It takes 46% less time per task. What’s Next After Huang? https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/huang-nvda-ai-startup-funding-record-2026/ Fri, 13 Nov 2026 20:32:55 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94391 Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026. The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data , already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor. With co-founder Jensen Huang ’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China , we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold. A widening investment footprint Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall. With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital , Atomico and Index Ventures , which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years . “Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi , a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.” Plural partners from left: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co. , which develops space transportation. More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum , which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute. Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi. “Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’ and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said. The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022. The team has two other partners: Carina Namih , co-founder of HelixNano , and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty , a former Uber executive. Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving bandwidth to work hands-on with founders. The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. Hark states that the gains come from reinforcement learning (RL) that penalized wasted turns and latency. For teams building browser agents, it is a case study in training for speed, not only accuracy. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Runs on: Hark’s cloud. Each request gets a dedicated virtual computer. Users reach it from web, iOS and Android. No local or quantized option. Bottom line (worst): Every Handoff² number is self-reported. No third-party score exists yet. What is Hark Handoff²? Handoff² is a computer-use agent from Hark that operates websites the way a person does. It clicks, types and scrolls on live pages instead of calling APIs. Hark previewed Handoff in August and shipped it in Hark Pro in October. Since then, Hark says it has logged over 5.6M browsing sessions and handled over $20M in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications. How does Handoff² get 2x faster? Hark co-evolved 2 things: the agent harness and the RL training recipe. The new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn. Training then penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency. The model learned 3 habits: Batch actions, such as filling several form fields in 1 turn. Group repeated action patterns into reusable composite actions. Reuse those composites as the task continues. Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, file system and terminal. The model outputs cursor and keyboard actions aimed at screen coordinates. Because savings stack per turn, gains grow on longer, browsing-heavy tasks. How fast is Handoff² compared with Handoff? Hark reports these speedups over v1 : Average: about 2x faster end to end. Flight booking: up to 3.8x faster. Long research tasks: more than 5x faster. Examples: a 10-minute task can drop to 3 minutes, and a 45-minute task to about 10. What do the Handoff² benchmarks show? Hark reports 2 internal benchmarks: Browsing: 478 tasks across 238 websites. Handoff² completes 82%, up from 73% for v1. It takes 46% less time per task. Hark ran Claude Opus 5.5 (max) in the same harness as Handoff². Handoff² lands within 5 points of it. Note that v1 was measured in its original harness, not the new one. Alignment: 93.8% for Handoff², up from 90.3% for v1. The suite checks that the agent never checks out without approval. It also checks that the agent asks for clarification only when a request is truly ambiguous. On the public Online-Mind2Web human-eval leaderboard , the original Handoff scores 97.67%. The LLM system writes tests designed to fail on risky diffs, and caught 74 privacy SEVs before landing in H1 2026, with a 60% engineer-reported true-positive rate. The post Meet Meta’s JiTTests: LLM-Generated Tests Designed to Fail Before Risky Code Lands appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Meta has moved Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) from research prototype into its production infrastructure . Meta JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change. A failing test is concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. The method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper ‘Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ‘. TL;DR Scale: Runs on Meta backend code with hundreds of millions of lines. The research paper analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Runs on: Meta’s internal infrastructure, overnight on spare capacity. Judge models in the paper: Llama3.3-70B, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4. Not publicly available. Performance: Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate at full scale (self-reported). Best: 74 privacy SEVs caught before landing in H1 2026; privacy SEV occurrence down 20%. Worst: The initial deployment confirmed only 8 of 41 reported catches (19.5%). Bottom line: Best: executable proof of a bug before merge. Worst: internal only, with self-reported numbers. What are Catching JiTTests? Catching JiTTests are LLM-generated tests that should fail when a diff introduces a bug. Traditional hardening tests pass when written and guard against future regressions. Catching tests target the change under review, before it lands. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper ‘Harden and Catch’ . Most AI bug tools act like faster human reviewers. They read the diff and leave comments. JiTTests instead execute code and show a concrete behavioral difference. Meta team concedes this takes more computational steps. It argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss. How does the JiTTests pipeline work? The production pipeline has 5 stages: Targeting: Runs overnight on spare capacity. It selects the previous day’s risky diffs, using a mechanism similar to Meta’s Diff Risk Score. Test generation: 2 diff-aware workflows produce candidate tests (explained below). LLM-as-Judge ensemble: Several LLMs score each failing test using the test code, failure trace, diff and inferred intent. RubFake: The Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment adds deterministic checks. Its rules flag patterns like reflection, broken mocks and not-implemented exceptions. Human-on-the-loop: The system decides whether to contact an engineer, based on the combined ranking. Dodgy diff vs intent-aware: what is the difference? The dodgy diff workflow assumes every diff is buggy. It treats the diff as a mutant of its parent and generates tests that tell them apart. The intent-aware workflow first infers what the diff should do from its code, title and summary. It lists risks, builds a mutant for each, and writes tests to kill them. Tests that then fail on the real diff become ‘weak catches.’ What do the benchmarks show? The research team analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Diff-aware methods produced 4x more candidate catches than hardening tests. They produced 20x more than tests that failed by coincidence. The intent-aware workflow produced weak catches in 6.4% of its tests and on 7.9% of diffs. Dodgy diff scored 2.5% and 4.0%. Meta’s earlier ACH mutation-guided hardening scored 0.8% and 1.6%. The rule-based and LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%. TestGen-LLM row uses the “need not add coverage” setting. A weak catch is a candidate failure, not a confirmed bug. What changed at full scale? The initial deployment was modest. Meta reported 41 candidate catches to engineers. 8 were confirmed true positives, a 19.5% rate. 4 of those would have caused serious failures in production. The October 2026 engineering post reports much stronger production numbers: 589 engineers engaged with JiTTests, 64% of those contacted. Engineers reported a 60% true-positive rate. 74 privacy SEVs were caught at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. Overall privacy SEV occurrence fell 20% in the same period. What does human-on-the-loop mean? Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews every output. Human-on-the-loop means engineers set criteria and monitor results in aggregate. They intervene at the policy level, not on each test. Meta team rarely need to read test code. They only confirm whether an observed behavior change was intended. Can developers use JiTTests? The answer is No. JiTTests is internal Meta infrastructure. Meta has not released code, models or an API. Teams can still copy the pattern: diff-aware mutation-guided test generation, an LLM judge ensemble, deterministic filters and aggregate human oversight. Key Takeaways Meta’s JiTTests writes LLM tests meant to fail on buggy diffs. 74 privacy SEVs caught pre-merge in H1 2026; privacy SEVs down 20%. Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate, up from 19.5% in the paper. Intent-aware tests hit weak catches at 6.4%, vs 0.8% for ACH hardening. Internal only: no code, model or API released. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Fri, 13 Nov 2026 20:50:40 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 VC Firm Plural Closes On $1.1B To Invest In European Startups With Potential For ‘GDP-Level Impact’ https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/plural-closes-billion-euro-fund-european-ai-robotics-defense-startup-investment/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 07:00:39 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94388 Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe. With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital , Atomico and Index Ventures , which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years . “Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi , a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.” Plural partners from left: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty. (Courtesy photo) Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy . In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica , whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co. , which develops space transportation. In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental , which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics , which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub , which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics , which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks . More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum , which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute. Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi. “Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’ and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said. The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022. Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026. The team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus , co-founder of Wise , and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport , both early employees at Skype , as well as Ian Hogarth , co-founder of Songkick , and Khaled Helioui , former CEO of Bigpoint . The team has two other partners: Carina Namih , co-founder of HelixNano , and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty , a former Uber executive. Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving bandwidth to work hands-on with founders. The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Fri, 13 Nov 2026 20:50:40 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 In The AI Era, Keep Hiring New College Grads — And Make Them Managers From Day One https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/new-college-grads-workforce-management-morse-strattam-quoia-kse/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 12:00:36 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94382 A few months ago, I was sitting lakeside with a neighbor. He is the head of AI for a pharmaceutical company, and he mentioned the truly incredible productivity his senior team is receiving from AI. Then he paused and turned to me and said: “You know, I may never hire another junior engineer again. Which is great for the business right now, but who’s the next generation that is going to run this when we retire?” The concern over what will happen to young people just entering the workforce is one many of us are grappling with right now, and it has a human dimension. Not just what happens to employment rates, but what happens to my students or my children? College graduates typically do the individual contributor knowledge work that AI is evermore capable of delivering. To cite one statistic , a recent Stanford study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to AI is running 19% below rates for their peers in less AI-impacted sectors, and that gap has been widening. What role will new graduates play in the age of AI? And how will we develop the generation of managers who will supervise AI? Fortunately, we have thriving examples with 200 years of history on how to teach 22 year olds to do exactly that. Our claim is that the reason senior folks get more out of AI today is not primarily because they have greater subject knowledge, but rather because they are good managers. They have to trust folks who work for them without completely trusting them, they have to divide tasks, delegate clearly, check results and patiently correct, coach, and sometimes shift personnel on their teams. The future for new graduates is to become great managers now, at the very beginning of their career, and not after a long period of individual contribution. The craft of management The nature of the innovation of AI is that it delivers knowledge work. We know a lot about human knowledge workers and the analogy to AI knowledge workers is strong. Knowledge workers know much more about their individual sphere of expertise than their managers do. Good managers routinely organize and lead knowledge workers who are just flat-out much smarter than they are. They do this through the craft of management. These same qualities, as AI behaves more like AI executives , naturally give good managers the skills to manage AI agents, who become the individual contributor knowledge workers. It is no secret that the investment industry culture values most highly the brilliance of the individual contributor who delivers the incisive observation, makes the correct investment call, and closes the one-on-one negotiation with a win. I have lived this culture for a long time. Calling an investor a “great people manager” is a backhanded compliment at best. In the investment industry, the jump from individual contributor to manager usually arrives midcareer or later, and typically with little to no formal training in the craft of management. The analyst, associate and vice president are primarily acting as individual contributors (though of course they may mentor a few junior folks), and are not shifting to acting primarily as managers of other knowledge workers until principal or perhaps partner. When I was an analyst at Morgan Stanley many years ago, the hierarchy ran from analyst to managing director. Analysts were the ultimate individual contributors, and whenever an analyst would attempt to delegate some work to others, we had a name for that: “managing analyst.” This clever put-down reflected the cultural belief that real credit goes to those who do, not those who deliver through the work of those they manage. What happens without management This blind spot on the importance of management is not limited to the investment industry. As another salient recent example, let’s look at the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident . Much has been written about this event, where OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face . In OpenAI’s own report on the incident, its proposed long list of fixes, including stronger security, alerts on breaches and post-incident remediation, does not address directly training its employees to be better managers of these agents. That’s even as the company acknowledges that members of an internal team at OpenAI knew of many of the concerning behaviors (including message board and unauthorized internet access) in late May, and did not act until July. This may be an unfair analogy, but imagine if we hired 1,200 workers to operate a warehouse complex, gave each of them detailed written instructions, and then had all the line managers and senior managers leave for a week. If we came back to find that someone had stolen a delivery van, the problem wouldn’t be that these weren’t the right workers or that the instructions weren’t clear enough. The problem is lack of management. Accelerated leadership development Michael Quoia, co-founder and partner at KSE Leadership. As I was wrestling with this problem, I talked with my business school classmate Michael Quoia, who attended the U.S. Naval Academy and served as an officer, and then built a career in executive leadership development. He recalled: “When I met my division of 25 sailors in Yokosuka, Japan at the young age of 22 years old, I was greeted by my senior chief petty officer, who already served for nearly 20 years. Behind him, we had several organizational levels including the first line sailors who conducted maintenance on the fire control systems. This was actually a harder problem than we are facing with AI. This was about supervising at least three levels without experience. I was expected to provide character, judgment, problem solving and leadership, despite not having come up through the ranks. How did the Navy develop these qualities in me so that I could bypass time in the seat as a frontline worker?” Like companies facing the AI dilemma we have been exploring, the military needs to develop capable leaders who lack entry-level experience. And while the military is a very relevant example, it is not the only one. The Home Depot ’s store management program and General Electric ’s Crotonville are two examples of corporations who recruit high-potential talent and put them through an accelerated leadership development program to prepare them to lead people in jobs they have not done. Let’s look, though, at how the Naval Academy provided Michael’s training, and what that may mean whether you are 22 years old or hiring 22-year-olds. First, the foundation of developing future officers is the development of moral leadership. The mission of the United States Naval Academy begins with the phrase “To develop midshipmen morally, mentally, and physically … .” In an age of AI, first-line managers of AI agents will need integrity and a moral compass, because AI does not come with that reliably pre-installed. It is no overstatement to suggest that moral leadership of AI could have societal implications and needs to be developed. Second, the service academies are intentionally designed as leadership laboratories. From plebe summer to commissioning, midshipmen progress from learning how to be a good subordinate to true manager. What is most relevant to the age of AI is that simulated leadership learning is possible and proven if designed with care.
